verdict.justification: Both deliverables recommend the same workable phased schedule: six days through week 13, five days in weeks 14–15, and regular four-day weeks from week 16. B is more decision-ready because it explicitly quantifies the week-10 exposure as approximately 23 standard hours and requests a management decision on temporary support or an agreed schedule change. It also provides formula-driven measures distinguishing the first zero-past-due week from sustained catch-up, making the eight-week recovery period clearer. A contains numerical and explanatory inconsistencies: its transition description says the buffer builds to approximately 90 hours, whereas the supplied demand and proposed capacity produce approximately 116.5 hours by the end of week 15. A’s email also incorrectly says demand stays above capacity through week 13, despite several intervening weeks having demand well below capacity. Both email drafts exceed the requested few sentences, but B’s clearer exception handling and more consistent recovery explanation make it the stronger deliverable.

decisive_issues.issue: The stated end-of-transition buffer is inconsistent with the proposed schedule and reference demand; it should be approximately 116.5 standard hours.
The email incorrectly describes demand as remaining above capacity throughout the catch-up period.
decisive_issues.quote: Cutting days sooner does not work because demand stays above capacity through week 13
